name: variable must appear in an actual declaration vs being inferable from use in the method body
side_a: No_deduct only when each required variable appears in an explicit declaration statement with the `private` modifier and a type at class level (e.g. `private double amount;`). Credit is given for the declaration itself, regardless of how correctly the variable is later used.
side_b: Deduct when a required variable is never declared anywhere and only shows up as a bare identifier inside a method (`amount = amount + used;`), even though its intended role as the remaining-amount field is obvious; an undeclared identifier is not a private instance variable.

name: Compile errors / type mismatches outside the constructor header: ignore (credit) vs propagate (deduct)
side_a: no_deduct — Award the point based solely on the constructor header matching `Bottle(double ____)`. Ignore errors located elsewhere: missing semicolons, undeclared fields used in other methods, or assigning the double parameter into an `int` field. These do not affect whether the required constructor header was written.
side_b: deduct — Withhold the point if the class contains any compile-breaking defect connected to the constructor, e.g. the parameter is a double but the field it is assigned to is declared `int` (lossy conversion), or the field assigned in the constructor is never declared.

name: Header declared with a return type (`public void Bottle(double)`): treat as satisfying the header (credit) vs treat as a method, not a constructor (deduct)
side_a: no_deduct — Credit the point as long as the declaration names `Bottle` and takes a single `double` parameter, even if a return type such as `void` is written before the name, since the required parameter list and name are present.
side_b: deduct — Withhold the point when a return type is declared (`public void Bottle(double capacity)`), because that is a method declaration rather than the required constructor.

name: Remaining-amount field never declared / never assigned in the constructor: credit capacity anyway vs. deduct for an incomplete constructor
side_a: Award the point as long as the constructor assigns the parameter to a properly declared capacity instance variable, even if the class never declares a remaining-amount instance variable at all and the constructor makes no assignment to it (the undeclared/uninitialized amount is penalized only under the instance-variable/method items, not here).
side_b: Deduct if the constructor does not initialize the full object state — i.e., if the remaining-amount instance variable is missing from the class or left unassigned by the constructor — on the grounds that the constructor is incomplete even though the capacity line itself is correct.

name: `void updateAmount(double x)` — `void` is an incorrect return type vs header otherwise acceptable
side_a: Deduct whenever the method is declared with a return type other than `double` in the literal sense of a non-numeric/no-value type — specifically `void`. `public void updateAmount(double used)` fails the 'returns double' requirement outright, regardless of the correct visibility, name, and single `double` parameter. Award the point only when the token immediately before `updateAmount` is `double`.
side_b: Do not deduct for `void` as long as `public`, the name `updateAmount`, and a single `double` parameter are present; treat the return-type requirement as satisfied by the method's intent to update the amount, and penalize the absent return value under the return/logic sub-item instead.

name: Subtraction actually assigned back to the amount field vs. no/incorrect stored update
side_a: If the method updates the field with a real assignment that subtracts the used quantity (e.g. `amount = amount - used;` or `this.currentAmount -= amountRemoved;`), give credit for the update step.
side_b: If the subtraction result is never stored in the field — a bare expression statement such as `amount - used;` — or the field is changed by the wrong operation (`amount = amount + used;`), withhold credit.

name: Refill test uses strict `<` one-quarter threshold vs. inclusive `<=`
side_a: If the refill condition compares strictly below a quarter of capacity (`amount < 0.25 * capacity`), give credit.
side_b: If the condition includes the boundary (`amount <= 0.25 * capacity`), so the bottle is refilled when exactly one quarter remains, withhold credit.

name: Body contains an actual return statement vs. method body never returns anything (falls off the end / declared void)
side_a: Do not deduct when the body of updateAmount contains an explicit return statement that hands back a numeric remaining-amount expression or variable (e.g., `return amount;`, `return this.currentAmount;`), regardless of whether the arithmetic or the update logic elsewhere in the method is correct.
side_b: Deduct when updateAmount contains no return statement at all — the method is declared `void` and simply mutates state, or it is declared to return a numeric type but the body ends after the if/else with no `return` — since no remaining amount is ever returned to the caller.
